content: The acceptable temperature range for conducting the test is between 2°C and 30°C. The required volume of the specimen depends on the type: 25 µL is needed for serum or plasma, while 50 µL is required for whole blood. The time required to test a single specimen is approximately 16 minutes. Certain equipment is necessary for the procedure but is not provided with the testing kit. This includes personal protective equipment (PPE) such as gloves, a lab coat, or a gown; a timer; appropriate biohazard waste containers; and specific tools for blood collection. For capillary blood collection, a lancet, cotton wool, and alcohol swab are required. For venous blood collection, venepuncture apparatus and suitable blood collection tubes are necessary. External quality assessment (EQA) is an inter-laboratory comparison designed to evaluate whether an HIV testing service can accurately determine the correct HIV status. EQA ensures that assays are performed with precision, results are reproducible, and errors are identified and corrected to prevent misdiagnosis or misclassification. EQA can involve observational visits, typically conducted by a site supervisor, to monitor testing practices. Supervisors must be trained and proficient in quality management principles and testing procedures. These visits should occur at least annually, though every three to six months is preferable. Another form of EQA involves participation in an external quality assessment scheme (EQAS), also known as proficiency testing programs. In this approach, a panel of blinded specimens is sent to a testing site, where they are processed according to standard procedures. The final HIV status and test results are then reported back to the EQAS provider for analysis. EQAS panels may consist of serum or plasma specimens collected clinically. However, the large volumes required for such specimens make this approach impractical for many programs. An alternative is the dried tube specimen (DTS) methodology, which involves mixing sera with green dye (to visualize the pellet) and allowing it to dry at the bottom of a tube. This method provides a practical and cost-effective way to prepare specimens for distribution to remote laboratories and testing services. For detailed instructions on preparing DTS panels, refer to the study by Parekh et al., titled Dried tube specimens: a simple and cost-effective method for preparation of HIV proficiency testing panels and quality control materials for use in resource-limited settings, published in the Journal of Virological Methods in February 2010. It is essential that any EQA activities include provisions for follow-up and corrective actions in response to unacceptable results. National reference laboratories should participate in international EQAS at least twice per year. Simultaneously, national laboratories should aim to conduct national EQAS for all testing services using locally derived and prepared DTS panels. The World Health Organization (WHO) is currently developing specific guidance on this topic.
